doc.title: Ruth Brown interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995

title: Race music and Randy's Record Shop radio
summary: Brown explains that R&B was called race music and reached far audiences through a white country DJ's station in Gallatin, Tennessee.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: You say though that this music, my thoughts of early rhythm & blues was that this music had something incredibly alive in it, because it was basically being sung and performed by black performers for predominantly black audiences.
So there was a communal effect there. Could you talk about that communal effect?
Could you talk about the music also being need-based?

Yeah, well the reason that what you say is very true is because at that time, when I first began recording, which was in 1948, the music that I sang or that other artists like myself, — Jackie Wilson, The Drifters, The Clovers, The Flamingos, Chuck Willis, Roy Brown, Charles Brown, Wynonie Harris, to name only a few — was referred to as race music. And it was not played by your top 100 stations. Basically, every southern town had a local radio station. The wattage wasn’t so powerful that you could hear what they played up north so to speak, but there was one station that was very responsible for this music being heard as far east and west as it was. And that was small radio station in Gallatin, Tennessee called Randy’s Record Shop. Now what was unknown to the listening public was that the disc jockey at that station was a country & western person. He was white, he was not black. But he had the love for this music. He had the most popular radio station that there was. It was called Randy’s Record Shop. And that is how the voice of Ruth Brown got to be heard as far as California, as far as Chicago, you know, all the midwest, even though I was basically located in Virginia, which was my state of origin.
